[[RunningHead]]

Reflexive violence

Christopher Scanlon and John Adlam

John Adlam

UK

UK

John Adlam  

self-harm, violence, personality disorder, subjection, social exclusion, systems-psychodynamic

In this article we build on a previous work to develop a critique of the notion of the supposedly deliberate or intentional quality of acts of self-harm and self-neglect. We suggest the term reflexive violence as a way to understand how some of us harm or neglect our-selves and become ‘identified’ as casualties (though not necessarily victims) of processes of inclusion/exclusion, oppression and colonisation played out between in-groups and socially constructed out-groups. We deploy this construct of reflexive violence to review shifting attitudes toward what constitutes deviance from the norm in modern societies, particularly the social and historical fluidities in the contested definitions of ‘personality disorder’ reflected in the American Psychiatric Association's periodic redrafting and updating of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual. We also draw on philosophical, sociological and historical sources to develop a psychosocial and systems-psychodynamic commentary on discourses of power whose modalities of domination may be perceived in this violent attribution of intent into the excluded out-group.

Henry Krips

Henry Krips

Henry Krips   About the AuthorHenry Krips is Andrew W. Mellon Chair of Humanities and Professor of Cultural Studies at Claremont (CA) Graduate University. He is author of The Metaphysics of Quantum Theory (Clarendon Press, 1989) and Fetish: An Erotics of Culture (Cornell University Press, 1999). He has co-edited collections on Science, Reason and Rhetoric (Pittsburgh University Press, 1995), Der Andere Schauplatz: Psychoanalyse, Kultur, Medien (Turia Kant, 2001) and Event and Process: Badiou, Deleuze and Whitehead (Cambridge Scholars Press, 2010). He is currently writing books on Cultural Politics and a rereading of Lacan's Seminar XI.
Lacan, gaze, pictures, radical politics

In chapter 8 of his Seminar XI, Lacan emphasizes the “pacifying Apollonian effect” of paintings, and again in chapter 9, he refers to their “calming,” “comforting” effects. In making these remarks, Lacan seems to spell doom for any radical cultural politics of the image. And, Joan Copjec points out, this is precisely how Lacan's work has been read by traditional Feminist Film Theory, which appropriates his theory of the gaze in order to show that cinematic images have a conservative effect in propping up the patriarchal order. In this paper, I argue against this reading of Lacan. In particular, I show that, in his remarks on the disruptive impact of the gaze, Lacan opens a space in which the picture may operate as a radical political tool.

Freud upside down: African American literature and psychoanalytic culture

Anthony Cooke

Anthony Cooke

USA

Anthony Cooke  

Badia Sahar Ahad University of Illinois Press, Urbana, 2010, 216pp., hardcover, $40.00, ISBN 978-0-252-03566-1

Most scholars of African-American literature view psychoanalytic theory as anathema. At best, black intellectuals dismiss psychoanalysis as irrelevant to their interests; at worst, many view it as an exclusively Western field designed to colonize or pathologize black cultural productions. Thus, a nuanced and productive integration of psychoanalysis and African American literary criticism remains, like race itself, an elusive task.

I am interested neither in disparaging scholars who have traditionally been hostile to psychoanalytic ideas nor in presenting myself as an apologist for racism or the misuses to which psychoanalysis has been put throughout the twentieth century and into our own day. Rather, I wish to insist here on the potential of psychoanalysis to generate useful criticism within African-American literary and cultural contexts, and, more to the point, to draw attention to the originality of Badia Sahar Ahad's study, Freud Upside Down: African American Literature and Psychoanalytic Culture. As a black literary critic whose primary methodology is psychoanalysis (in particular Freudian and Lacanian), I welcome Ahad's intervention. Regrettably, her book stands as only the second major work (besides Claudia Tate's Psychoanalysis and Black Novels: Desire and the Protocols of Race, published over ten years ago) seriously to consider the possibilities for African-American literature latent in psychoanalytic theory. Whereas Tate (1998) focused on desire and its articulation outside of racially inflected or revolution-oriented confines, Ahad moves both deeper within African-American literature and farther outside it. She skillfully merges author biography with racial textual analysis to recover the underappreciated tradition of black authors and critics who not only knew about psychoanalysis, or who simply referred to it in their works, but also who saw its relevance for black culture, including those who actively sought out collaboration with psychoanalysts.

There have been numerous attempts to link discourse analysis and psychoanalytic theory over the past two decades, be it within the remit of postcolonial or cultural studies, or under the auspices of discursive psychology. It has proved difficult to find a mid-way between the epistemic push-and-pull of these two approaches. Such attempts have often resulted in the assimilation of psychoanalytic ideas into the terms of rhetorical or textual analysis. Billig's (1999)Freudian Repression is perhaps the signal example of such a re-writing of Freudian notions within the vocabulary of discursive psychology. A particular challenge comes into view here: how might the properly psychoanalytic dimension of Freudian concepts be retained in such contexts, how might we avoid compromising their unique explanatory value, especially given the post hoc tinkering typically required of a post-structuralist sensibility?

Added to these problems is the fact that psychoanalytic – and particularly Lacanian – excursions into the domain of discourse theory tend to result in forms of theoretical abstraction less than conducive to the work of applied empirical analysis. The work of Ernesto Laclau signals a vital bridge here, and it is no surprise that the early sections of Claudia Lapping's excellent Psychoanalysis in Social Research make extended reference to Laclau in suggesting a series of psychoanalytic directions for psychosocial research. That Lapping writes from within psychosocial studies helps. This discipline, an ever-rejuvenating articulation of the sociological and the psychical, is at home both with forays into theory, and the requirements of empirically-based research projects. The crucial link between Laclau and Freudian theory identified by Lapping is the notion of overdetermination. The book's second chapter features a wonderfully textured account of Freudian dream theory – a rich and under-utilised resource for text analysis – that is alive to the nuances and complexities of Freud's thinking. In reply to Dr. Singer, I question whether clinicians have a monopoly on understanding the unconscious. I reiterate the contention that if clinicians are to engage in cultural analysis, they need to be aware of the epistemology and methodology of disciplines whose sole purpose is to understand culture. The demanded self: Levinasian ethics and identity in psychology

Rebecca Mitchell

Rebecca Mitchell

USA

Rebecca Mitchell  

David M. Goodman Duquesne University Press, Pittsburgh, PA, 2012, 290pp., $30.00, ISBN 978-0820704494

Where, in the current terrain of psychoanalytic practice, is there room for the ethics demanded of the self by the other? In The Demanded Self: Levinasian Ethics and Identity in Psychology, David M. Goodman surveys the critical and practical landscape of psychoanalysis, notes the absence of ethics, and turns to the phenomenology articulated by twentieth-century philosopher Emmanuel Levinas for a corrective. Levinas, Goodman argues, provides the grounding for a psychology that would not only make room for ethics, but that would fully embrace the ethical imperative by placing the other – as opposed to the self – at its centre. This is not entirely new ground. Among others, C. Fred Alford, George Kunz, Paul Marcus, and Richard N. Williams have taken on wide-ranging reassessments of psychoanalysis in light of Levinas’s oeuvre. Though informed by such work, Goodman extends the grasp of a Levinasian psychoanalysis by suggesting that psychology must be reoriented from the constructs of selfhood that have long defined it. Following Levinas’s phenomenological account of the unbridgeable asymmetry of the other in relation to the self, such a reorientation would lead, Goodman argues, to a psychology inherently more alive to ethics.

In the introduction to The Demanded Self, Goodman frames Levinas’s philosophy in contrast to the Western, post-Enlightenment tradition, and in relation to the psychological models generated from that tradition. The alignment of psychologies around scientific epistemologies has been essential, he argues, in according “legitimacy and prestige” (p. 8) to the field and its practical application. But though psychology’s embrace of science has helped legitimize its practice, Goodman suggests that the universality vaunted by scientific epistemology obscures alterity. Otherness that does not conform to a universally agreed-upon truth must not be truth; such conclusions obviate the ethical response demanded from the self by the other.

Lebanese civil war, memory, trauma, archive, affect, art

This paper turns to Rabih Mroué's Make Me Stop Smoking, a one-man multimedia performance, for its capacity to enable us to think about the dilemmas of narrativizing the Lebanese civil war. Critical of Lebanon's official position to move on and forget the war, Mroué presents his audience with his unofficial and personal archive of war, collected over the years without any purpose in mind. His archive consists of random objects, fragments of memory, which speak more to his affective relationship than to the certainty of his experience. Contradiction, hesitation, and pain are what organize his narrative. Indeed, what Mroué delivers to his audience is the vulnerable and fallible human in history. The audience is invited to witness the singularity of a man torn by a nagging memory of his own complicity in the war. Mroué's Make Me Stop Smoking is an invitation to visit the archive and be suspicious of its desires. Archival objects, left unexamined, have the power to construct and stabilize narratives. Hence, a living archive, argues the author, requires an interest in death and in mourning the objects to which one becomes inflexibly attached.

Computers and databases, mobile telephony and SMS texting, the Internet and email, digital broadcasting and satellites: all such mobile technologies feed directly into the performativity of mobile lives. Yet digital technologies also facilitate the mobilization of feelings and affect, memories and desires, dreams and anxieties. This mobilization is very complex and contradictory at the level of the self. Lita Crociani-Windland Anthem, London, 2011, hardcover, 224pp., $99.00, ISBN-13: 978-0857289988

The ethnographic fabric of this book consists of case studies of festivals in the province of Siena, Italy: the Palio of Siena, Montepulciano's Bruscello Theatre and Bravio Delle Botti (Barrel Race), and Monticchiello's theatre. The approach is Deleuzian.

It is easy to use, apply and fake Deleuze these days, with a growing body of texts to draw on and a continuing appetite for studies on affect. What is infinitely harder to do -- what cannot be faked -- is ‘a Deleuzian apprenticeship’ in which ethnographic research, theory, time, place, tradition, history, people, forces, powers, communities, cultural events and personal insight illuminate and support one another, producing assemblages of great intellectual, methodological and emotional interest. Such assemblages never fail to draw readers into apprenticeships of their own. Lita Crociani-Windland's book does just that.

As the author explains in the introduction, each case study can be read independently. Their combined effect, however, constitutes the full apprenticeship. The case of the Sienese Palio horse race, which I will present here in some detail as an example of the book's approach, opens with an eye-witness account of the two-day event. This is followed by a detailed discussion of the historical dynamics of the region and the power struggles that gave rise to the system of contrade, the districts/neighbourhoods that are today represented in the race. The religious aspect of the festival, the use of animal emblems, the reasons for the change (from a long race to racing around the perimeter of the central square) and the boundary restrictions of the past are meticulously documented -- and so is the spirit of the Sienese people, their pride and sense of independence. The Deleuzian paradigm of ‘The State and the War Machine’ encompasses this web of forces. Through its lens, the race is seen as emerging from harnessing opposing forces, namely, those of an emerging army typical of the State, and the contrade, which remain mobile and fluent and typical of the War Machine. But the race is more than a creative way of settling and commemorating power struggles. It is an opportunity for Deleuzian becoming, which is always anti-authoritarian, anti-institutional and anti-masculine. Thus, this highly charged and ‘manly’ race is shown to have a great affinity with a process of transformation, a becoming-animal, which has found its way into the emblems of the contrade and a becoming-child, which is confirmed in the status of the winning side as the city's beloved ‘child’. The complex analysis offered by the author exceeds the confines of a single methodological approach or discipline but is clearly shown to have benefited from several. The analysis also illuminates ways in which the present is connected to the past, generations to one another and identity to cultural belonging -- without identity being restricted by cultural belonging.

Hurricane Katrina, disaster relief, trauma, psychological first aid

The most disadvantaged New Orleans residents were stranded in the city when the levees broke in the wake of Hurricane Katrina. The author, a psychoanalytic clinician, encountered some of these victims as a first responder in the Red Cross shelters in Dallas, TX. Psychological first aid in such situations involves shoring up defenses and promoting resilience. Clinical and organizational vignettes demonstrate a psychoanalytic approach to psychological first aid and disaster response. Three trauma theories (Bowlby's attachment theory, Hobfoll's conservation of resources theory and Strozier's “ground zero” theory) are used to understand the trauma experienced by those in Dallas shelters.

Ross Truscott

South Africa

Derek Hook Routledge, London, 2012, 264 pp., hardcover, £57.00/paper £19.99/digital £19.95, ISBN 9780415587563/9780415587570/9780203140529

The practice of critical psychology is usually defined in two ways: as the internal critique of the discipline of psychology, and as the various kinds of analytical work done by politically committed psychologists. Derek Hook's (2012) recent book, A Critical Psychology of the Postcolonial: The Mind of Apartheid addresses two notable gaps in the critical psychology literature, the first of which is postcolonial studies. The second gap, curious for a branch of psychology, is psychological forms of analysis. The influence of poststructuralism in this second gap should not be underplayed; under the influence of the work of Foucault amongst others, there has taken place in critical psychology, as in other disciplines, a shift towards a focus on the sociohistorical constitution of the subject, as well as a cultivation of suspicion over deployments of “psychological operations – as psychological operations,” (Hook, 2007, p. 60).

There are very good reasons for this second gap, chief among them the psychological reductionism that plagued many earlier forms of social psychology. But, as Hook (2012) argues, “warnings against the perils of psychological reductionism too often provide the excuse to dismiss from serious consideration the psychological dimension of colonial power” (p. 97). If subjectivities are not merely the effect of colonial and neocolonial distributions of power, but are also its conduits, its channels of transmission, then how, Hook asks – mindful of the risk of psychological reductionism – might “the radical potential of types of psychological critique” (p. 15) be set to work in addressing social problems like racism? In this regard the focus point of the book is South Africa, and the bulk of the examples to which Hook refers come from the Apartheid Archive (AA), a research project that aims to amass a series of personal narratives remembering life during apartheid.

Psychoanalytic listening to socially excluded young people

Miriam Rosa and Ilana Mountian

Ilana Mountian

UK

Brasil

Ilana Mountian   bimountian@yahoo.com
psychoanalytic listening, socially excluded young people, transference, resistance

Individuals excluded from ‘the social contract’ are subject to a certain irruption of the traumatic, understood as subjective disorganization resulting from the emergence of that which is outside sense and outside signification. Such subjects experience the loss of a discourse of belonging and of being afforded a place in society. The lack of narcissistic gratification, along with the exclusion from group ideals and values, foster a fragmentation of social ties and produce disruptive effects in subjectivity. This paper discusses the possibilities afforded by psychoanalytic listening to subjects who have experienced social exclusion as traumatic: those who suffer extreme poverty and social exclusion within neoliberal economic models. Examples are drawn from clinical work with young people who live on the outskirts of the city of São Paulo and who have had the experience of living in the streets. Rather than attuning to this sort of listening, it is not rare for those in some social agencies and in some forms of psychotherapy to mistake apathy, loneliness and muting for structural characteristics of the subject rather than as the effects of exclusion and the reproduction of a form of social violence. This misrecognition precludes the creation of a symbolic elaboration that could provide a symptomatic shape to that which is experienced as traumatic. This paper argues for the possibility of listening to subjects silenced by exclusion.

In his late work, Michel Foucault finds in Greek antiquity a form of subjectivity that makes no reference to a universal law. The virtual world of cyberspace appears to offer individuals a similar possibility, in which the fundamental limitations that form the subject in the external society no longer apply. However, this article argues that the universal law actually is more powerful in cyberspace, insofar as it remains outside of our capacity for recognizing it. Nevertheless, the redeeming possibility of cyberspace lies not in what cyberspace promises, but rather in its capacity to makes palpable our inevitable failure to achieve the promise of complete, digital satisfaction.

This field note is a first attempt to reflect on the choreography of the European crisis from a psychosocial perspective. It focuses on the situation as it has been unfolding in one of the debtor countries of the South, namely Greece. This paper attempts a new theoretical synthesis for studying ‘moral panics’. Its proposed model ties together Bion's psychoanalytic theory of the development of collective emotions with Foucault's discourse theory, particularly his account of the role of the moral code in the cultivation of subjectivity. Stephen Barber  

Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, Jonathan Goldberg (ed.) Duke UP (Series Q), Durham, NC, 2011, 240pp., $23.95, ISBN-13: 978-0822351580 (paperback)

Posthumously published in 2011, The Weather in Proust gathers together the late work – mostly unpublished talks and essays – of the eminent literary critic and leading figure in the development of queer theory Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick. The first of its three sections belongs to the work that Sedgwick was writing on Proust, mysticism and psychology at the time of her untimely death from cancer in 2009, and its five chapters provide a rich sense of what that book was to have been. The second section is comprised of three chapters in which she reflects on the present state of queer culture and thought. In the book’s third section, a single chapter titled “Reality and Realization,” Sedgwick expands on many of the themes – existential, mystical, and affective – that preoccupied her throughout this last period of her life. Famous for her heuristic practice of speaking in the first person singular as she broke through to new possibilities for intellectual life, and famous, as well, for her readings of literary texts, here, in her last work, Sedgwick presents an “I” who speaks with the same brilliance but now, provoked by the news of certain mortality, out of the need to practice emptiness and nonbeing creatively.

Beginning with a reading of the narrator’s remarkable relationship to atmosphere in Proust’s À la recherche du temps perdu, the chapters in the first section range from insightful reflections on the surprising appearance of “queer little gods” in Proust’s novel and the poetry of C.P. Cavafy to a rich meditation on Sedgwick’s own practices as a writer and artist. The section concludes with a powerful critique of cognitive science’s “theory of mind,” which Sedgwick develops through an exceptionally attentive and sympathetic interpretation of the affective experience of autism. What is striking in the selections in the second section of the volume is Sedgwick’s dismay at the present amnesia regarding AIDS in gay mainstream culture and, no less significant for her, an amnesia in queer theory regarding the critical/creative resources that came out of the AIDS activisms of the 1990s. In a chapter on Melanie Klein in the first section, Sedgwick attributes the paranoid element of 1990s queer theorizing – her own included – to the culturally pervasive sense of dread and unknowingness prompted by the public scandals, official silence, and panic around AIDS. Significantly for the general temper of the volume, she reflects on how news of her own emergency in 1996, when she learned that the breast cancer she had been diagnosed with in the early 1990s had spread and become incurable, was met with a different, reparative impulse.

The present special issue highlights the individual contributions, innovative research and therapeutic interventions outside the office of two generations of psychoanalysts. Taking testimony; interviewing; documentary film-making; social activism; and direct clinical interventions in communities suffering disaster and chronic social trauma: these are among the varied kinds of innovative work presented by the contributing authors. Many psychoanalysts today are bringing their analytic perspective and clinical skills into contexts far beyond the traditional office setting; some even take psychoanalysis beyond strictly defined therapeutic settings. The articles in this special issue illustrate the range of concerns and types of intervention that this kind of work can entail when engaging with trauma. Dori Laub   About the AuthorDr. Dori Laub was born in Cernauti, Romania on June 8, 1937. He is currently a practicing psychoanalyst in New Haven, Connecticut who works primarily with victims of massive psychic trauma and with their children. He is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the Yale University School of Medicine and co-founder of the Fortunoff Video Archive for Holocaust Testimonies.
traumatic experience, testimonial interpretation, the internal “Thou”, narrativization

At the very core of the extreme traumatic experience (for example, genocide or childhood sexual abuse) is the obliteration of the internalized, empathic communicative dyad. Just as the executioner does not heed the pleas for life and relentlessly proceeds with the execution, the internal “Thou,” the addressee with whom inner dialogue takes place – a prerequisite to symbolization and to internal world representation – ceases to exist. Without that internal dialogue, psychic representation of the traumatic experience cannot exist and narrative cannot be formed to relate it to another. Therefore, to a large extent, the witness “does not know” what she knows of her experience of extremity. It is only through the testimonial process, in the company of an intimate, totally present listener, that the lost internal “Thou” can begin to be reestablished and the process of internal dialogue, symbolization, and narrative formation can resume. A memory is thus created that can be both related and forgotten. The (video) testimonial intervention described here has a therapeutic effect by both creating a remembered past and freeing up the emotional space for present living. Trauma discourse is replete with failed attempts at narrativization of trauma, ranging from momentary lapses, through dissociative states, to total muteness. Examples of such “crises of witnessing” will be given.

Sociologists engaging with depth psychology have rarely drawn on the work of C. G. Jung. Part of the reason for this, I suggest, is Jung’s seeming tendency to credit, and be informed by, religious and non-rational perspectives. In this article I first highlight what sociologists might find problematic in Jung by comparing his views on the desacralisation of the modern world with Max Weber’s views on disenchantment. I then argue that Charles Taylor’s recent alternative account of disenchantment and secularity provides a framework within which Jung’s thought becomes more sociologically creditable despite, and even because of, its approach to matters of religion.

In the writing on play for which he is best known, the British psychoanalyst D.W. Winnicott (1971) did more than theorize the role of transitional objects in the life of children. He also cleared a space in psychoanalytic theory for nonpathological states, activities, and forms of relatedness. He wrote:

Starting as we do from psychoneurotic illness and with ego defences related to anxiety that arises out of the instinctual life, we tend to think of health in terms of the state of ego defences. We say it is healthy when these defences are not rigid, etc. But we seldom reach the point at which we can start to describe what life is like apart from illness or absence of illness. That is to say, we have yet to tackle the question of what life is about. (p. 133)

What makes us, Winnicott asks, “begin to be, to feel that life is real, to find life worth living”? (ibid.). The contemporary psychoanalyst Christopher Bollas, a prolific writer with more than a dozen books to his name, takes up these questions throughout his work, pursuing not only “creative living” in adult life, but also the extraordinary creativity of the unconscious mind, whose processes are always operating but seldom directly recognized – even, he argues, by psychoanalysis itself. The Christopher Bollas Reader collects some of his best essays, including two pieces new for this volume. It also includes a useful introduction by Arne Jemstedt, comprising a brief biography of Bollas, a summary of his central concepts, and a complete list of his publications.

In Bollas's work, the unconscious is not simply the inert place of the repressed. Rather, the unconscious is imagined as a process of both reception and generation – it is an endlessly ramifying “intelligence of form.” Playing on Freud's phrase “the psychopathology of everyday life,” Bollas studies instead its “psychocreativity,” especially as we encounter the work of the unconscious in dreams, in the way we use objects to build and transform ourselves, and in the analytic process (Bollas is particularly interested in free association and the analyst–analysand couple he calls the Freudian Pair).

R.J. Lifton, psychoanalysis, activism, psycho-history, group identity

Renowned psychiatrist and social activist Robert Jay Lifton considers his life and career in a conversation with two psychoanalysts. Looking back on the major early influences on his psychoanalytically informed ideas and research methods, Lifton talks about his analytic training, his later involvement with the Wellfleet group, most particularly Erik Erikson, and his experience as a psychiatrist in Japan and China in the post–World War II period of “American triumphalism.” Lifton discusses some of his major concepts in relation to a psychoanalytic perspective, including his notions of “ideological totalism” and “survivor guilt and mission,” and the power that ideology and group pressures have in a particular historical context to transform individual identity and psychology.

Although reality TV’s presentation of authenticity has been contested since the genre emerged at the turn of the century, discourse dedicated to debunking its halfhearted claim to the real continues to persist. This article adopts a psychoanalytic framework to explain this compulsion in the context of a broader ideological disposition that finds enjoyment in the detection of artifice. To do this, it examines reality TV from the perspective of Lacan’s discussion of the eye and trompe-l’oeil to argue that reality TV is appealing because its depictions of authenticity can so easily be (mis)recognized as (im)possible.

old age, affect, transitional phenomena, ritual, repetition

This paper develops a psycho-social understanding of difficult and disabling life transitions, particularly in relation to old age. The paper brings together a biographical case study and theoretical analysis that draws on three sources: the work of Deleuze and Bergson in continental philosophy, Winnicott in psychoanalysis, and Turner in anthropology. By linking experience, theory and practice, I show how different, but related concepts, at different levels, may shed light on some puzzling behaviour common in old age. More broadly, I point to the value of such theoretical work for understanding and managing traumatic affect and life transitions.

He is the Director of the MA in Jungian and Post-Jungian Studies and a member of the Executive Committee of the International Association for Jungian Studies.
analytical psychology, cultural complex, methodology, psychohistory, history

This paper explores the nature of interdisciplinary research in psychoanalytic studies by critically assessing the theory of cultural complexes. Too often, ‘applied psychoanalysis’ becomes ‘wild psychoanalysis’ when interventions ignore the respective epistemologies and methodologies of the disciplines onto which depth psychological theories are being applied. The notion of cultural complexes is one such case. The claim that the idea is a uniquely Jungian contribution to understanding culture is challenged. Important methodological hurdles that arise when a psychology of the individual is mobilized to explain group phenomena are ignored, as are its debts to the discipline of history. Perhaps most problematic is how the theory potentially sustains a tyrannical framework whereby different ways of remembering a past are stifled.
